<mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--1" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Which style do you want to choose?<div><ul><li>Carolingian</li><li>Romanesque</li><li>Gothic</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="140" width="180" x="170" y="-220" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell value="Carolingian<div>Binding</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="120" x="130" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-2" edge="1" parent="1" value="Romanesque Binding" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="120" x="760" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--17" parent="1" style="shape=hexagon;perimeter=hexagonPerimeter2;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fixedSize=1;" value="Gothic Binding" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="120" x="1400" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--21" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Carolingian bindings typically begin with binding the upper wooden board, or cover, to the book block (the stack of quires). First, choose a shape for the book board. What kind of edge will it have?<div><ul><li>&nbsp;square edges</li><li>&nbsp;slightly bevelled edges</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="120" width="300" y="110" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--22" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="26" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="40" y="250" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--23" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="27" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="190" y="250" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-70" edge="1" parent="1" source="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--24" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=0.5;exitY=1;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;entryX=0.5;entryY=0;entryDx=0;entryDy=0;" target="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--25"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-71" edge="1" parent="1" source="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--24" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=0.75;exitY=1;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;entryX=0.5;entryY=0;entryDx=0;entryDy=0;" target="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--27"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--24" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Before binding to the book block, channels have to be drilled into your board. Vegetable cord supports will be laced into the board, and later bound to the book block (the stack of quires). How will your boards be drilled? We have two options:<div><ul><li>pattern 1</li><li>pattern 2</li></ul>The dotted lines represent internal channels through which the sewing supports or endband supports will be laced.&nbsp;</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="150" width="420" x="-90" y="350" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-68" edge="1" parent="1" source="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--25" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=0.5;exitY=1;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;" target="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--32"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--25" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="33" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" y="530" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-69" edge="1" parent="1" source="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--27" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=0.5;exitY=1;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry"> <mxPoint x="120.00000000000023" y="830" as="targetPoint" /> </mxGeometry> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--27" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="34" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="100" y="530" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--32" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="The board has been drilled to fit three sewing supports. Since those sewing supports will be laced into the board and then sewn to the book block, the book block has to have holes in it for the thread. Will the holes be cut in, as with a knife or chisel, or pierced, as with an awl or needle?<div><ul><li>pierced</li><li>cut</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="130" width="520" x="-140" y="830" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--33" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="10" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="-20" y="990" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--34" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="11" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="150" y="990" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--35" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="The sewing supports are lined up along the three inner rows of holes. The outer rows at the head and tail of the spine is where the thread that is being woven between the quires and the sewing support will change direction. This is called a change-over station. We're going to use the common herringbone stitch for the sewing support, but you need to decide what kind of stitch you want to use at the change-over:<div><ul><li>link stitch</li><li>span stitch</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="130" width="490" x="-180" y="1090" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--36" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="16, without quire layer, 21+22" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="90" width="90" x="-20" y="1230" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--37" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="16, without quire layer, 23+24" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="150" y="1230" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--39" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="<div><br></div>After the sewing supports have been bound to the book block, the free ends of the sewing supports are laced into the lower book board. They are drawn through pre-drilled channels and pegged in place. Now endleaves are pasted to the inside book covers. You have three options:&nbsp;<div><ul><li>no endleaves</li><li>use the first and last pages of the book block</li><li>add a thin additional quire</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="200" width="400" x="-100" y="1460" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--40" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="no change" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="-50" y="1680" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--41" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="no change" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="100" y="1680" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--42" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="1 + 2,<div>top and bottom leaves</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="240" y="1680" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--43" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="After this, the edges of the whole book are trimmed. This may have been done with a drawknife or perhaps a file. The pages and even the book cover itself become even. The wooden book board sometimes show traces of this trimming.<div>Are you ready to trim?</div><div><ul><li>yes</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="120" width="380" x="-70" y="1830" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="zrRwhkcnBDUkeFU7xrb--44" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Now the spine has to be reinforced. To do this, a piece of leather or alum-tawed leather was pasted onto the spine. Room had to be allowed for the sewing supports. Choose what form it should have:&nbsp;<div><ul><li>no spine lining</li><li>patch lining, pasted between the sewing supports</li><li>a full sheet of lining with windows cut out for the sewing support</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="170" width="440" x="-150" y="2100" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-1" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="no change" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="-40" y="2310" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-2" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="39" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="60" y="2310" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-3" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="40" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="160" y="2310" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-5" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="To reinforce the fragile spine, the quires were sewn together at the top and bottom. Often a tab of leather or alum-tawed leather was added to do this. We will use a tab. Sometimes a cable was added along the very edge. We will use an endtab. Now decide whether you:<div><ul><li>will use no cable support</li><li>will use a double cable support</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="160" width="390" x="-100" y="2400" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-6" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="The free edge of the endtab is trimmed to a square shape or to a round shape.&nbsp;<div><ul><li>square</li><li>round<span style="background-color: transparent; text-wrap-mode: nowrap; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0); font-family: monospace; font-size: 0px; text-align: start;">r3CmxGraphModel%3E%3Croot%3E%3CmxCell%20id%3D%220%22%2F%3E%3CmxCell%20id%3D%221%22%20parent%3D%220%22%2F%3E%3CmxCell%20id%3D%222%22%20parent%3D%221%22%20style%3D%22ellipse%3BwhiteSpace%3Dwrap%3Bhtml%3D1%3Baspect%3Dfixed%3B%22%20value%3D%22%22%20vertex%3D%221%22%3E%3CmxGeometry%20height%3D%2280%22%20width%3D%2280%22%20x%3D%22-40%22%20y%3D%222310%22%20as%3D%22geometry%22%2F%3E%3C%2FmxCell%3E%3C%2Froot%3E%3C%2FmxGraphModel%3Err</span><span style="background-color: transparent; text-wrap-mode: nowrap; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0); font-family: monospace; font-size: 0px; text-align: start;">%3CmxGraphModel%3E%3Croot%3E%3CmxCell%20id%3D%220%22%2F%3E%3CmxCell%20id%3D%221%22%20parent%3D%220%22%2F%3E%3CmxCell%20id%3D%222%22%20parent%3D%221%22%20style%3D%22ellipse%3BwhiteSpace%3Dwrap%3Bhtml%3D1%3Baspect%3Dfixed%3B%22%20value%3D%22%22%20vertex%3D%221%22%3E%3CmxGeometry%20height%3D%2280%22%20width%3D%2280%22%20x%3D%22-40%22%20y%3D%222310%22%20as%3D%22geometry%22%2F%3E%3C%2FmxCell%3E%3C%2Froot%3E%3C%2FmxGraphModel%3Es</span></li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="120" width="280" x="-66" y="2657" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-7" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="47" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="10" y="2570" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-8" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="48" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="130" y="2570" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-9" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="52" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="10" y="2800" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-10" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="53" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="130" y="2800" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-11" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="At this time, the leather cover will be pasted on to the book boards. At the same time a piece of the cover is sewn together with the endtab. Choose a stitch:<div><ul><li>link stitch</li><li>saddle stitch</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="140" width="330" x="-150" y="2920" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-12" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="If 52 above, then<div>***</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="-90" y="3080" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-13" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="55" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="110" y="3170" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-14" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Finally the leather had to be cut and neatly trimmed on the inside covers. This formed mitred corners. Are you ready to mitre the corners?<div><ul><li>yes</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="115" width="330" x="-60" y="3265" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-15" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Finally, a fastening was attached. In the Carolingian period, this fastening was usually made of a leather strap, metal attachment, and metal eyelet that would fit around a peg on the bottom cover.&nbsp;<div>Are you ready to add the fastening now?</div><div><ul><li>yes</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="130" width="270" x="-60" y="3495" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="s0KuCaGF3YptCOnIi6Y_-16" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="57" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="70" y="3395" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-1" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="<span style="color: rgb(255, 255, 255); font-family: Helvetica; font-size: 12px; font-style: normal; font-variant-ligatures: normal; font-variant-caps: normal; font-weight: 400; letter-spacing: normal; orphans: 2; text-align: center; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; white-space: normal; background-color: rgb(27, 29, 30); text-decoration-thickness: initial; text-decoration-style: initial; text-decoration-color: initial; display: inline !important; float: none;">Your quires are stacked on top of one another. It is time to decide how many sewing supports you will bind the book with. This book block will be designed for three sewing supports, and they will be equally spaced, since that was the most common design. Since those will be sewn to the book block, the book block has to have holes in it for the thread. Will the holes be cut in, as with a knife or chisel, or pierced, as with an awl or needle? This was probably done while the quires were held tight in a press.</span><div><ul><li><span style="color: rgb(255, 255, 255); font-family: Helvetica; font-size: 12px; font-style: normal; font-variant-ligatures: normal; font-variant-caps: normal; font-weight: 400; letter-spacing: normal; orphans: 2; text-align: center; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; white-space: normal; background-color: rgb(27, 29, 30); text-decoration-thickness: initial; text-decoration-style: initial; text-decoration-color: initial; display: inline !important; float: none;">cut</span></li><li><span style="color: rgb(255, 255, 255); font-family: Helvetica; font-size: 12px; font-style: normal; font-variant-ligatures: normal; font-variant-caps: normal; font-weight: 400; letter-spacing: normal; orphans: 2; text-align: center; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; white-space: normal; background-color: rgb(27, 29, 30); text-decoration-thickness: initial; text-decoration-style: initial; text-decoration-color: initial; display: inline !important; float: none;">pierced</span></li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="170" width="460" x="560" y="110" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-3" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="9" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="700" y="300" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-4" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="8" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="880" y="300" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-5" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Now you have to decide whether to add endleaves. When included, these were additional wraps for the book block. Sometimes they were glued down to the inside cover, almost always after the book board had been covered with leather or another material. Will you:<div><ul><li>use no endleaves</li><li>use the first and last pages of the book block</li><li>add a thin additional quire</li><li>wrap the whole book block in a large bifolium</li></ul>The form could vary, particularly of the additional quire. Sometimes it was a folio with a stub. Finally, front and back endleaves could be treated differently.<br><br></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="220" width="430" x="560" y="400" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-6" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="no change" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="620" y="682" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-7" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="1+2" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="830" y="682" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-11" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="no change" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="730" y="682" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-12" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="3" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="930" y="682" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-15" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="The quires are now ready to be bound together. They will be sewn together along three sewing supports, which will later be laced into the book boards. These sewing supports are made of alum-tawed leather and measured about 8-20 mm in width. Will you choose:<div><ul><li>a strap that has been slit down the middle</li><li>a strap that has been twisted&nbsp;</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="140" width="350" x="645" y="830" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-16" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="12A<div>Slit leather A</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="680" y="990" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-17" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="14A Twisted<div><br></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="840" y="990" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-16" edge="1" parent="1" source="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-18" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=0.75;exitY=1;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;entryX=0.5;entryY=0;entryDx=0;entryDy=0;" target="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-20"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-18" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="The sewing supports are suspended on the crossbar of the sewing frame. We are not quite sure how they were suspended, but some supports show slits or holes with traces of iron rust. The needle will draw thread through each quire and wrap around the sewing support. The change-over station at either end of the spine is where the thread shifts direction and travels back. In the Romanesque period, the change-over seems to have generally been done with a link stitch. What kind of stitch will you choose for the main sewing support?<div>If you chose a slit leather strap, you can now choose:<br><div><ul><li>herringbone</li><li>straight</li></ul>If you chose a twisted leather strap, you can choose:<br><ul><li>packed straight</li></ul></div></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="200" width="640" x="440" y="1080" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-12" edge="1" parent="1" source="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-19" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=0;exitY=1;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;" target="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-8"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-13" edge="1" parent="1" source="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-19" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=1;exitY=1;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;entryX=0.5;entryY=0;entryDx=0;entryDy=0;" target="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-9"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-19" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="If 12A, then" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="685" y="1300" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-14" edge="1" parent="1" source="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-20" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=0.5;exitY=1;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;" target="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-10"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-20" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="If 14A, then" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="880" y="1300" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-25" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="The book block is laid aside as preparing the book boards begins. Oak was common. Romanesque boards were typically slightly thicker at the spine, and the corners of the spine head and tail were cut, or "back-cornered," at a slant to accommodate the endbands . In addition, the edges of the board could be:<div><ul><li>squared</li><li>sightly beveled</li><li>rounded</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="180" width="290" x="690" y="1752" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-26" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="29" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="685" y="1960" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-27" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="31" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="920" y="1960" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-28" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="30" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="800" y="1960" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-29" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Channels must now be drilled into the boards so that the sewing supports can be laced through the board's spine edge and held in place with a wedge, peg or nail. Here are two patterns found repeatedly in one study of Romanesque binding:&nbsp;<div><ul><li>Type I</li><li>Type II</li></ul>Both lacing channels enter the board on the side. In Type I, the lacing channel is relatively short; in type II, relatively long. The endband support cable could also be laced into the board. These support cables are then laced into the boards and pegged in place.</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="150" width="720" x="480" y="2051" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-30" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="35" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="720" y="2207" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-31" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="36" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="900" y="2207" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-32" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="As reinforcement, a lining of chamois leather, textile or parchment could be pasted down along the spine. Wooden pegs could also be used if the lining was being fastened into the wooden board.<div>What will you choose?</div><div><ul><li>no lining</li><li>patch lining, made up of material "patches" placed between the sewing supports</li><li>a full-length, slotted lining with spaces cut out for the sewing supports</li></ul>In reality, multiple linings could be used, even on top of one another.</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="210" width="312.5" x="727.5" y="2440" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-33" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="39<div>on top of 81, 82, or 83, wherever it was left</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="830" y="2660" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-34" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="no change" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="680" y="2660" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-35" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="40<br><div style="forced-color-adjust: none; box-shadow: none !important; color: rgb(255, 255, 255); font-family: Helvetica; font-size: 12px; font-style: normal; font-variant-ligatures: normal; font-variant-caps: normal; font-weight: 400; letter-spacing: normal; orphans: 2; text-align: center; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; white-space: normal; background-color: rgb(27, 29, 30); text-decoration-thickness: initial; text-decoration-style: initial; text-decoration-color: initial;">on top of 81, 82, or 83, wherever it was left</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="970" y="2660" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-37" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="<font style="color: rgb(237, 237, 237);">Now that the book block is sewn together and the boards laced, the spine edges will be reinforced with endbands. Endband sewing links the quires together at the spine's top and bottom. A tab is placed at the top and bottom of the spine as a lining. It was often supported along the spine corner by a single or by a double cable, often of the same material as the sewing support, such as alum-tawed leather. Here are three options:&nbsp;</font><div><font style="color: rgb(237, 237, 237);"><br></font></div><div><p class="MsoListParagraphCxSpFirst" style="margin: 0in 0in 0.0001pt 35.45pt; line-height: 16.8667px; font-family: Arial, sans-serif; text-align: start; text-indent: -0.25in;"></p><ul><li><font style="color: rgb(237, 237, 237);">Double support </font><font style="color: rgb(237, 237, 237);">with</font><font style="color: rgb(237, 237, 237);"> straight packed stitching</font></li><li><font style="color: rgb(237, 237, 237);">Double support with herringbone stitching</font></li><li><font style="color: rgb(237, 237, 237);">Single support with straight packed stitching</font></li></ul><font color="#ededed">Sometimes the stitching could embroidered with a second layer of coloured linen or silk, but this was less common before the fourteenth century.</font></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="250" width="380" x="660" y="2760" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-38" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="49 on top of previous step" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="695" y="3031" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-39" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="<span style="color: rgb(255, 255, 255); font-family: Helvetica; font-size: 12px; font-style: normal; font-variant-ligatures: normal; font-variant-caps: normal; font-weight: 400; letter-spacing: normal; orphans: 2; text-align: center; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; white-space: normal; background-color: rgb(27, 29, 30); text-decoration-thickness: initial; text-decoration-style: initial; text-decoration-color: initial; display: inline !important; float: none;">48 on top of previous step</span>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="825" y="3031" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-40" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="50 on top of previous step" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="965" y="3031" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-42" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="The top of the endband tab is then trimmed, perhaps mostly round, but sometimes squared. Which will you choose?<div><ul><li>square</li><li>round</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="130" width="310" x="740" y="3130" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-43" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="52" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="740" y="3280" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-44" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="53" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="915" y="3280" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-22" edge="1" parent="1" source="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-45" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=0;exitY=0.75;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;entryX=0.5;entryY=0;entryDx=0;entryDy=0;" target="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-21"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-25" edge="1" parent="1" source="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-45" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=0.5;exitY=1;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;entryX=0.5;entryY=0;entryDx=0;entryDy=0;" target="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-20"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-45" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="The book boards were then covered, most often in a pale white or grey chamois or alum-tawed leather or with a red or brown vegetable-tanned leather. The latter was preferred if the book was to receive blind-tooled decoration. A starch paste was common. On the inside boards, the covering was typically cut at the corners, or "mitred", and the edges were sewn together, as shown below. In addition, the covering was sewn together with the endband tab. What stitching style will you choose?<div><ul><li>link stitch</li><li>saddle stitch</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="190" width="330" x="780" y="3380" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-46" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="55, link" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="870" y="3647" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-47" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="56, saddle" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="980" y="3647" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-48" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Finally, a fastening could be fashioned. A leather strap, sewn together of two leather pieces, was generally used. It was nailed into the side near the free edge of one of the covers, generally the upper cover. An eyelet or hasp of bronze or iron was attached to the end. Sometimes it was decorated with geometric, floral or animal designs. It had a hole that fit around a peg on the opposite cover. If a short strap is used, it joins to a peg projecting from the edge of the opposite board. This edge-fashioning is inherited from the Carolingian period and preferred in Germany and Central Europe. If a long strap is used, it wraps around to a peg laid into the side of the opposite cover. This form dominates after 1200 and in French and English bindings. Which will you choose?<div><ul><li>short strap</li><li>long strap&nbsp;</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="210" width="440" x="690" y="3745" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-49" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="63" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="790" y="4010" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-50" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="64" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="950" y="4010" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-51" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Here you have your cover. Sometimes a fixed or loose overcover was added to wrap the book in, as illustrated below. Of course the cover could also be painted or decorated in various ways.&nbsp;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="100" width="270" x="790" y="4197" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="firS6Iq-pWCEXIFt7hlh-53" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="By designing a Gothic book cover, you undertake a book that may be different in an important way: it is increasingly probable that your quires are made of paper. First you have to decide where to place the sewing holes. Unlike the previous periods there seems to be a connection between the number of sewing stations, the length of the spine and the thickness of the book. Moreover, the outer segments between the change-over stations and the head or tail vary quite a lot in size. Would you like to:<div><ul><li>cut the holes</li><li>pierce the holes</li></ul>Piercing was more common in England and after 1450.</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="230" width="410" x="1240" y="120" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-1" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="11" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1300" y="370" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-2" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="10" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1510" y="370" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-3" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="You also have to decide about the endleaves, which help fix the book block to the book boards. Do you want:<div><ul><li>to use no endleaves</li><li>to use the first and last pages of the book block</li><li>to add a thin additional quire</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="120" width="350" x="1275" y="490" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-4" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="1+2" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1550" y="630" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-5" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="no change" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1420" y="630" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-6" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="no change" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1280" y="630" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-7" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="The material of the sewing supports becomes more diverse in the late Middle Ages. Vegetable cords, often doubled, were more common, as well as leather straps, usually white alum-tawed leather, not vegetable tanned-leather. Slit leather straps were quite common, as well as intertwisted slit straps where one end was twisted several times through through the slit. These are suspended from the sewing frame.&nbsp;<div>Which will you choose?</div><div><ul><li>split leather strap</li><li>double vegetable cord</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="180" width="380" x="1290" y="730" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-9" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="13A, double cord" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1560" y="930" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-10" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="12A" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1360" y="930" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-11" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="For the changeover station, the link stitch comes to predominate over the simple span stitch. Nevertheless, a more innovative solution to spine sewing is also available: integral sewing. Integral sewing was known in the Romanesque period, and was slightly more widespread in the Gothic period, while still representing a very narrow part of all bookbindings. This technique eliminated the change-over station along the spine and treated the change-over in the same step as the endband. This undoubtedly sped up work. It meant that the endband was added at the same time as spine sewing and that the change in direction took place at the endband. Would you like to use:<div><ul><li>the link stitch at the change-over station</li><li>integral sewing</li></ul><span style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));"><div style="text-align: left;"><span style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));">Integral sewing means that the endband will not be added later. Secondary embroidery was usually not used over integral endband stitching.&nbsp;</span></div></span></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="300" width="370" x="1330" y="1030" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-12" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="84" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1545" y="1340" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-13" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="21+22 on top of 11 or 10, as chosen above" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1410" y="1340" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-41" edge="1" parent="1" source="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-14" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=1;exitY=0.25;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;entryX=0.5;entryY=0;entryDx=0;entryDy=0;" target="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-40"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-44" edge="1" parent="1" source="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-14" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=0;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=0;exitY=0.25;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;entryX=0.5;entryY=0;entryDx=0;entryDy=0;" target="szKMXe_X-YJ2N9GKZuXr-39"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-14" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;align=left;" value="The sewing thread probably becomes thinner in the late Middle Ages. Hemp is used more and more against the use of of flax in earlier days. After the mid-fifteenth century packed straight sewing along the sewing supports became frequent, but other options were possible. Choose which you would like to use:<div><ul><li>herringbone sewing</li><li>packed straight sewing</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="150" width="370" x="1310" y="1450" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-15" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="18, straight packed" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1200" y="1630" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-17" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Scholars conjecture about the next steps. It seems that animal glue was sometimes used on the spine to reinforce a sewing technique made weaker by thin thread. Second, it seems that the spine was deliberately given a convex shape by blows from a hammer or other tool, whereas Carolingian and Romanesque spines were either flat or concave. This procedure apparently reduced swelling at the spine triggered by the use of thread. Some spines show accidental marks left by the rounding tool. Finally, the spine was lined with a parchment or leather. Several styles of lining were available: patch lining, spine-width linings placed between the sewing supports; transverse linings, also placed between sewig supports, but wider than the spine and later glued to the inner or outer faces of the boards; a full-lenth strip with&nbsp; holes cut out to allow for the sewing supports; two comb linings that overlapped one another. Which lining would you like?<div><ul><li>patch lining</li><li>comb lining</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="270" width="440" x="1270" y="1730" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-18" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="85,<span style="background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));">&nbsp;on top of the book block as it was left</span>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1570" y="2040" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-19" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="39, on top of the book block as it was left" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1320" y="2030" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-20" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Now the book block was trimmed. Unlike earlier binding, it now took place before the boards were attached. This was probably done with a long, flat-bladed drawknife, a binder's plough, or, very rarely, a file. The plough held the book block steady as a blade was repeatedly drawn across the edges. The book block had to be carefully positioned, so that it would form right angles at the corners. The first evidence for this device comes from 1530, but some marks left on late fifteenth-century book block edges match those left on sixteenth-century books that were undoubtedly trimmed with a plough.<div>Are you ready to trim the edges?</div><div><ul><li>yes</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="195" width="470" x="1260" y="2155" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-21" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="69,&nbsp;<div>this needs to be set under all the other things</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="105" width="105" x="1440" y="2355" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-22" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="If you used integral sewing earlier on, you will skip this step, in which endbands are added. If you chose integral sewing, you have already added endbands. The endband is a stitch that links the quires together at the top and bottom of the spine, reinforcing the binding at the spine edges. Often the sewing takes place along a cable support running across the top or bottom spine width of the book. In the Gothic period, this seems to have been mostly a single cable with straight packed sewing, whereas a double cable was also used in earlier periods. The majority seem not have used a tab lining. There were many types of endband in the Gothic period. Some endbands were later sewn together to the back cover; decorative embroidery could be added to them. Time-consuming as it was, short-cuts were employed, such as reducing the number of stitches or using colored thread at the start to achieve an embroidered appearance without a second stitching campaign. Which will you choose?<div><ul><li>Skip this. I used integral sewing</li><li>single support cable with straight packed sewing</li><li>endband sewing with additional embroidery sewing</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="220" width="610" x="1260" y="2480" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-23" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="In this period, the wooden boards used for the cover are usually oak or beech. Pine, walnut, and others also appear. The supports entered the board not from the edge as in Romanesque binding, but from the board's outer face. Thus the spine edge was generally rounded or bevelled in order to easily enter. It could also be beveled or rounded on the inside to allow for the shoulder of the book block. If bevelling was applied on the free edges, it could appear at any point on either face. Parts that might be decorated or might be outfitted with fastenings might not be bevelled at all. Would you like to see the board now?<div><ul><li>yes</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="200" width="370" x="1400" y="2990" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-24" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="27" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1560" y="3200" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-26" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="The sewing supports were regularly laced from the outside of the board and fitted into channels that travelled to the inside of the board. Sometimes the channels were extended further toward the middle of the board. Or, this was done for some sewing supports, but not all of them. The staggered positing of the holes and channels prevented the boards from later splitting all the way through. Choose whether the laces will be drawn through evenly drilled or staggered channels:<div><ul><li>evenly drilled channels</li><li>channels with staggered lengths</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="183" width="380" x="1370" y="3297" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-27" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="38" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1620" y="3520" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-28" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="37" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1430" y="3510" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-29" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Now the cover was pasted onto the boards. It was generally leather, but Gothic bindings show greater variety in the type of leather. Textiles were also used. Chamois leather became more common than alum-tawed leather. Pig skin, sheep skin and calf skin were all used. A vegetable paste (e.g., flour) was used, but there is some evidence for animal glue. The leather had to be pulled tightly onto the board, with key incisions allowing for folds and sometimes scoring the wooden boards to create a more adhesive surface. The cover was turned into the inner cover at the corners and cut, or mitred, from the corner to remove material and create a neat angle. The leather could be stained both before and after this process. Overcovers could also be added: a leather protective cover; a textile overcover or sleeve called a chemise; an overback, that is, an additional covering along the spine and fastened to the edges of the book board." vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="190" width="460" x="1310" y="3610" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-33" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="86" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1537.5" y="2760" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-34" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="87" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1670" y="2760" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-35" parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;aspect=fixed;" value="?" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="80" width="80" x="1510" y="3840" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="xmXUCECXKlNbeyTVbRs0-36" parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;" value="Finally, a fastening was applied. It could take the form of a Romanesque long strap, in use until the end of the Middle Ages, or the hook clasp, which appears around 1400. The long strap was a two-layered leather strap anchored near the free edge of&nbsp; board. It was outfitted with an eyelet or grommet that would fit over a peg on the opposite board. The hook clasp was made up, on one board, of an anchor for a leather strap with a shallow metal hook attached to it, and, on the opposite board, of a catch plate over which the hook would fit. We have three kinds of hook clasp for you to choose from.<div><ul><li>long strap</li><li>English hook clasp</li><li>Dutch hook clasp</li><li>German hook clasp</li></ul></div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry div.div:
Carolingian bindings typically begin with binding the upper wooden board, or cover, to the book block (the stack of quires). First, choose a shape for the book board. What kind of edge will it have?
square edges
slightly bevelled edges

div.div:
Before binding to the book block, channels have to be drilled into your board. Vegetable cord supports will be laced into the board, and later bound to the book block (the stack of quires). How will your boards be drilled? We have two options:
pattern 1
pattern 2The dotted lines represent internal channels through which the sewing supports or endband supports will be laced.

div.div:
The board has been drilled to fit three sewing supports. Since those sewing supports will be laced into the board and then sewn to the book block, the book block has to have holes in it for the thread. Will the holes be cut in, as with a knife or chisel, or pierced, as with an awl or needle?
pierced
cut

div.div:
The sewing supports are lined up along the three inner rows of holes. The outer rows at the head and tail of the spine is where the thread that is being woven between the quires and the sewing support will change direction. This is called a change-over station. We're going to use the common herringbone stitch for the sewing support, but you need to decide what kind of stitch you want to use at the change-over:
link stitch
span stitch

div.div:
After the sewing supports have been bound to the book block, the free ends of the sewing supports are laced into the lower book board. They are drawn through pre-drilled channels and pegged in place. Now endleaves are pasted to the inside book covers. You have three options:
no endleaves
use the first and last pages of the book block
add a thin additional quire

Are you ready to trim?

no spine lining
patch lining, pasted between the sewing supports
a full sheet of lining with windows cut out for the sewing support

will use no cable support
will use a double cable support

Finally, a fastening was attached. In the Carolingian period, this fastening was usually made of a leather strap, metal attachment, and metal eyelet that would fit around a peg on the bottom cover.
Are you ready to add the fastening now?

div.span: Your quires are stacked on top of one another. It is time to decide how many sewing supports you will bind the book with. This book block will be designed for three sewing supports, and they will be equally spaced, since that was the most common design. Since those will be sewn to the book block, the book block has to have holes in it for the thread. Will the holes be cut in, as with a knife or chisel, or pierced, as with an awl or needle? This was probably done while the quires were held tight in a press.

Now you have to decide whether to add endleaves. When included, these were additional wraps for the book block. Sometimes they were glued down to the inside cover, almost always after the book board had been covered with leather or another material. Will you:
use no endleaves
use the first and last pages of the book block
add a thin additional quire
wrap the whole book block in a large bifoliumThe form could vary, particularly of the additional quire. Sometimes it was a folio with a stub. Finally, front and back endleaves could be treated differently.

a strap that has been twisted

div.div:
The sewing supports are suspended on the crossbar of the sewing frame. We are not quite sure how they were suspended, but some supports show slits or holes with traces of iron rust. The needle will draw thread through each quire and wrap around the sewing support. The change-over station at either end of the spine is where the thread shifts direction and travels back. In the Romanesque period, the change-over seems to have generally been done with a link stitch. What kind of stitch will you choose for the main sewing support?
If you chose a slit leather strap, you can now choose:
herringbone
straightIf you chose a twisted leather strap, you can choose:
packed straight

The book block is laid aside as preparing the book boards begins. Oak was common. Romanesque boards were typically slightly thicker at the spine, and the corners of the spine head and tail were cut, or "back-cornered," at a slant to accommodate the endbands . In addition, the edges of the board could be:
squared
sightly beveled
rounded

Channels must now be drilled into the boards so that the sewing supports can be laced through the board's spine edge and held in place with a wedge, peg or nail. Here are two patterns found repeatedly in one study of Romanesque binding:
Type I
Type IIBoth lacing channels enter the board on the side. In Type I, the lacing channel is relatively short; in type II, relatively long. The endband support cable could also be laced into the board. These support cables are then laced into the boards and pegged in place.

As reinforcement, a lining of chamois leather, textile or parchment could be pasted down along the spine. Wooden pegs could also be used if the lining was being fastened into the wooden board.
What will you choose?
no lining
patch lining, made up of material "patches" placed between the sewing supports
a full-length, slotted lining with spaces cut out for the sewing supportsIn reality, multiple linings could be used, even on top of one another.

div.font: Now that the book block is sewn together and the boards laced, the spine edges will be reinforced with endbands. Endband sewing links the quires together at the spine's top and bottom. A tab is placed at the top and bottom of the spine as a lining. It was often supported along the spine corner by a single or by a double cable, often of the same material as the sewing support, such as alum-tawed leather. Here are three options:

p.style: margin: 0in 0in 0.0001pt 35.45pt; line-height: 16.8667px; font-family: Arial, sans-serif; text-align: start; text-indent: -0.25in;

li.font: Single support with straight packed stitching

div.font: Sometimes the stitching could embroidered with a second layer of coloured linen or silk, but this was less common before the fourteenth century.

The book boards were then covered, most often in a pale white or grey chamois or alum-tawed leather or with a red or brown vegetable-tanned leather. The latter was preferred if the book was to receive blind-tooled decoration. A starch paste was common. On the inside boards, the covering was typically cut at the corners, or "mitred", and the edges were sewn together, as shown below. In addition, the covering was sewn together with the endband tab. What stitching style will you choose?
link stitch
saddle stitch

div.div:
Finally, a fastening could be fashioned. A leather strap, sewn together of two leather pieces, was generally used. It was nailed into the side near the free edge of one of the covers, generally the upper cover. An eyelet or hasp of bronze or iron was attached to the end. Sometimes it was decorated with geometric, floral or animal designs. It had a hole that fit around a peg on the opposite cover. If a short strap is used, it joins to a peg projecting from the edge of the opposite board. This edge-fashioning is inherited from the Carolingian period and preferred in Germany and Central Europe. If a long strap is used, it wraps around to a peg laid into the side of the opposite cover. This form dominates after 1200 and in French and English bindings. Which will you choose?
short strap
long strap

div.div:
By designing a Gothic book cover, you undertake a book that may be different in an important way: it is increasingly probable that your quires are made of paper. First you have to decide where to place the sewing holes. Unlike the previous periods there seems to be a connection between the number of sewing stations, the length of the spine and the thickness of the book. Moreover, the outer segments between the change-over stations and the head or tail vary quite a lot in size. Would you like to:
cut the holes
pierce the holesPiercing was more common in England and after 1450.

div.div:
The material of the sewing supports becomes more diverse in the late Middle Ages. Vegetable cords, often doubled, were more common, as well as leather straps, usually white alum-tawed leather, not vegetable tanned-leather. Slit leather straps were quite common, as well as intertwisted slit straps where one end was twisted several times through through the slit. These are suspended from the sewing frame.
Which will you choose?
split leather strap
double vegetable cord

div.div:
For the changeover station, the link stitch comes to predominate over the simple span stitch. Nevertheless, a more innovative solution to spine sewing is also available: integral sewing. Integral sewing was known in the Romanesque period, and was slightly more widespread in the Gothic period, while still representing a very narrow part of all bookbindings. This technique eliminated the change-over station along the spine and treated the change-over in the same step as the endband. This undoubtedly sped up work. It meant that the endband was added at the same time as spine sewing and that the change in direction took place at the endband. Would you like to use:
the link stitch at the change-over station
integral sewing
Integral sewing means that the endband will not be added later. Secondary embroidery was usually not used over integral endband stitching.

The sewing thread probably becomes thinner in the late Middle Ages. Hemp is used more and more against the use of of flax in earlier days. After the mid-fifteenth century packed straight sewing along the sewing supports became frequent, but other options were possible. Choose which you would like to use:
herringbone sewing
packed straight sewing

div.div:
Scholars conjecture about the next steps. It seems that animal glue was sometimes used on the spine to reinforce a sewing technique made weaker by thin thread. Second, it seems that the spine was deliberately given a convex shape by blows from a hammer or other tool, whereas Carolingian and Romanesque spines were either flat or concave. This procedure apparently reduced swelling at the spine triggered by the use of thread. Some spines show accidental marks left by the rounding tool. Finally, the spine was lined with a parchment or leather. Several styles of lining were available: patch lining, spine-width linings placed between the sewing supports; transverse linings, also placed between sewig supports, but wider than the spine and later glued to the inner or outer faces of the boards; a full-lenth strip with holes cut out to allow for the sewing supports; two comb linings that overlapped one another. Which lining would you like?
patch lining
comb lining

div.div:
Now the book block was trimmed. Unlike earlier binding, it now took place before the boards were attached. This was probably done with a long, flat-bladed drawknife, a binder's plough, or, very rarely, a file. The plough held the book block steady as a blade was repeatedly drawn across the edges. The book block had to be carefully positioned, so that it would form right angles at the corners. The first evidence for this device comes from 1530, but some marks left on late fifteenth-century book block edges match those left on sixteenth-century books that were undoubtedly trimmed with a plough.
Are you ready to trim the edges?
yes

div.div:
If you used integral sewing earlier on, you will skip this step, in which endbands are added. If you chose integral sewing, you have already added endbands. The endband is a stitch that links the quires together at the top and bottom of the spine, reinforcing the binding at the spine edges. Often the sewing takes place along a cable support running across the top or bottom spine width of the book. In the Gothic period, this seems to have been mostly a single cable with straight packed sewing, whereas a double cable was also used in earlier periods. The majority seem not have used a tab lining. There were many types of endband in the Gothic period. Some endbands were later sewn together to the back cover; decorative embroidery could be added to them. Time-consuming as it was, short-cuts were employed, such as reducing the number of stitches or using colored thread at the start to achieve an embroidered appearance without a second stitching campaign. Which will you choose?
Skip this. I used integral sewing
single support cable with straight packed sewing
endband sewing with additional embroidery sewing

div.div:
In this period, the wooden boards used for the cover are usually oak or beech. Pine, walnut, and others also appear. The supports entered the board not from the edge as in Romanesque binding, but from the board's outer face. Thus the spine edge was generally rounded or bevelled in order to easily enter. It could also be beveled or rounded on the inside to allow for the shoulder of the book block. If bevelling was applied on the free edges, it could appear at any point on either face. Parts that might be decorated or might be outfitted with fastenings might not be bevelled at all. Would you like to see the board now?
yes

The sewing supports were regularly laced from the outside of the board and fitted into channels that travelled to the inside of the board. Sometimes the channels were extended further toward the middle of the board. Or, this was done for some sewing supports, but not all of them. The staggered positing of the holes and channels prevented the boards from later splitting all the way through. Choose whether the laces will be drawn through evenly drilled or staggered channels:
evenly drilled channels
channels with staggered lengths

div.div: Now the cover was pasted onto the boards. It was generally leather, but Gothic bindings show greater variety in the type of leather. Textiles were also used. Chamois leather became more common than alum-tawed leather. Pig skin, sheep skin and calf skin were all used. A vegetable paste (e.g., flour) was used, but there is some evidence for animal glue. The leather had to be pulled tightly onto the board, with key incisions allowing for folds and sometimes scoring the wooden boards to create a more adhesive surface. The cover was turned into the inner cover at the corners and cut, or mitred, from the corner to remove material and create a neat angle. The leather could be stained both before and after this process. Overcovers could also be added: a leather protective cover; a textile overcover or sleeve called a chemise; an overback, that is, an additional covering along the spine and fastened to the edges of the book board.

div.div:
Finally, a fastening was applied. It could take the form of a Romanesque long strap, in use until the end of the Middle Ages, or the hook clasp, which appears around 1400. The long strap was a two-layered leather strap anchored near the free edge of board. It was outfitted with an eyelet or grommet that would fit over a peg on the opposite board. The hook clasp was made up, on one board, of an anchor for a leather strap with a shallow metal hook attached to it, and, on the opposite board, of a catch plate over which the hook would fit. We have three kinds of hook clasp for you to choose from.
long strap
English hook clasp
Dutch hook clasp
German hook clasp
